query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with density below 6 g/cm3, non-equilibrium solid solution regions formed during rapid induction melting will preferentially decompose into stable intermetallic compounds (such as Mg-rich phases and Al-rich intermetallics) upon thermal exposure. This structural evolution increases microstructural heterogeneity, leading to localized galvanic coupling that accelerates corrosion and high-temperature oxidation rates compared to the initial metastable solid solution baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Induction-melted Mg-containing lightweight HEA (e.g., MgAlCuZnGd or AlMgₓTiSnZn) in a non-equilibrium, predominantly solid solution state with density <6 g/cm3.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal annealing or exposure to elevated temperatures (e.g., 300–600°C) for sufficient time to allow phase transformation.
generation.conditions: Ambient or oxidizing environments; comparison between as-cast (non-equilibrium) and thermally exposed (transformed) states; density maintained below 6 g/cm3.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of stable intermetallic compounds and increased microstructural heterogeneity (e.g., Mg-rich and Al-rich intermetallics, phase boundaries).
generation.mechanism: Decomposition of metastable solid solution regions into stable intermetallics creates local electrochemical potential differences, promoting galvanic corrosion and facilitating oxygen diffusion at phase boundaries during oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thermally transformed alloy will exhibit higher corrosion rates and faster high-temperature oxidation (e.g., greater mass gain, oxide scale formation) than the as-cast, non-equilibrium baseline.
generation.baseline: Corrosion and oxidation behavior of the as-cast, non-equilibrium solid solution Mg-containing HEA.
generation.boundary: Prediction applies to alloys with density <6 g/cm3, containing Mg and other elements prone to intermetallic formation; does not apply if alloy remains a homogeneous solid solution after thermal exposure.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of corrosion and oxidation rate increase depends on specific alloy composition and thermal exposure parameters; exact phase assemblage may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples in as-cast (non-equilibrium) and thermally annealed (transformed) states. Subject both to identical corrosion (e.g., immersion in NaCl solution) and high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., exposure to air at 500°C). Measure corrosion rate (mass loss, electrochemical tests) and oxidation rate (mass gain, oxide scale thickness).
measurements: Oxidation rate (mass gain, oxide scale thickness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally transformed alloy does not exhibit higher corrosion and oxidation rates than the as-cast baseline, or if microstructural heterogeneity does not increase, the hypothesis is falsified.
